title: Original blue ink and decreasing negative effects
diagnosis: Earlier translation called the original blue ink purple and rendered a decreasing negative effect as a decaying effect.
correction: Original blue ink is restored. The negative effect becomes more negative over time; it does not necessarily decay toward zero.

title: What fixed effects actually control
diagnosis: The blue claim says all characteristics are controlled.
correction: Unit fixed effects absorb time-invariant differences between units; time fixed effects absorb shocks common to units at a given time. They do not control arbitrary unit-specific, time-varying confounders. Additivity and the identification assumptions still matter.

title: Define the cohort-time estimand
diagnosis: The written ATT expression is shorthand and does not specify a cohort-conditioned target.
correction: A precise version is \(\operatorname{ATT}(g,t)=E[Y_t(g)-Y_t(\infty)\mid G=g]\) for a treated cohort \(g\) and a post-adoption time \(t\). State whether treatment starts at \(t=g\) or only after it. An overall ATT requires aggregation weights.

title: Double demeaning needs the grand mean
diagnosis: Both original displays omit the grand mean and count T+1/N+1 observations while dividing by T/N.
correction:
For a balanced panel indexed by \(i=1,\ldots,N\), \(t=1,\ldots,T\), use
\[
\widetilde z_{it}=z_{it}-\bar z_{i\cdot}-\bar z_{\cdot t}+\bar z_{\cdot\cdot},\qquad z\in\{Y,D\}.
\]
Here \(\bar z_{i\cdot}=T^{-1}\sum_{s=1}^Tz_{is}\), \(\bar z_{\cdot t}=N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^Nz_{jt}\), and \(\bar z_{\cdot\cdot}=(NT)^{-1}\sum_{j,s}z_{js}\). The added grand mean makes each row and column mean zero. Omitting it shifts each transformed variable by a constant; if the final regression includes an intercept, the slope is unchanged. It is nevertheless not the exact fixed-effect residual, and a no-intercept regression need not give the same slope. With unbalanced panels, use the actual fixed-effect projection rather than this simple formula.

title: Strict exogeneity and DiD assumptions
diagnosis: The notebook groups several assumptions under strict exogeneity; they are not generally equivalent.
correction: In a static fixed-effect regression, a standard condition is \(E[e_{it}\mid D_{i1},\ldots,D_{iT},\gamma_i]=0\) (with the other regressors also conditioned on). Parallel trends and no anticipation are potential-outcome restrictions used for DiD; they are not interchangeable with the whole list. Dynamic effects can be allowed by changing the model and estimand.

title: The direction-of-bias claim refers to the illustrated comparison
diagnosis: The broad sign rule needs the specified comparison and dynamic-effect pattern.
correction: The sketch explains contamination when already-treated units serve as controls. The sign and magnitude of the aggregate TWFE discrepancy depend on cohort effects, their dynamics, and the regression weights; the illustration is not a universal sign theorem.

title: A complete lead/lag regression
diagnosis: The original expansion has inconsistent tail indices and no common time effects despite being introduced as TWFE.

title: Event-time dummies alone do not solve heterogeneous effects
diagnosis: Calling this a partial improvement is sensible, but an ordinary TWFE event study remains vulnerable to cohort heterogeneity.
correction: With staggered adoption and heterogeneous effects, a lead or lag coefficient can combine effects from other relative periods, and apparent pretrends can arise from effect heterogeneity. Use an estimator with explicit valid cohort comparisons when interpreting these coefficients causally.

title: Write cohort-by-time indicators explicitly
diagnosis: As written the sums reuse the observation indices and multiply every coefficient by the same Dit.
correction:
For observation \((i,s)\), the intended expansion is
\[
Y_{is}=\alpha_i+\theta_s+
\sum_{g\in\mathcal G}\sum_{t\geq g}\tau_{g,t}
\mathbf1\{G_i=g\}\mathbf1\{s=t\}+e_{is}.
\]
The cohort and calendar-time indicators are essential. This repairs the displayed notation, not the identification assumptions.

title: Control cohorts must supply untreated comparisons
diagnosis: The numeric rule g<q is a grouping convention and cannot by itself identify valid controls.
correction: If \(g\) is an actual adoption date, an earlier cohort may already be treated and cannot automatically serve as an untreated control. Use never-treated units, or not-yet-treated units during the relevant comparison window, with the appropriate parallel-trends and no-anticipation assumptions. The handbook example labels cohorts that adopt after the observed window as controls.

title: The four-block matrix needs a common treatment block
diagnosis: Absorbing treatment alone does not imply that all treated units share an adoption date.
correction: The displayed four-block representation assumes a common pre/post split for the included treated units. Under staggered adoption, construct valid cohort or period subpanels first, as in the later notes.

title: Allow zero donor weights
diagnosis: The handwritten SC and SDID constraints use strict positivity.
correction: The standard simplex constraint is \(w_i\geq0\), \(\sum_{i\in\mathrm{co}}w_i=1\), and similarly \(\lambda_t\geq0\), \(\sum_{t\in\mathrm{pre}}\lambda_t=1\). Zero weights are allowed. The open simplex \(w_i>0\) can exclude the optimizer. On pp. 8 and 10 the handwritten constraints additionally omit the summation sign: individual weights are not all equal to one. The formulas below restore the intended sum-to-one constraint.

title: Put the intercept in the design matrix
diagnosis: The source instruction says to add a row of ones before the outcome vector.
correction:
For the unit-weight fit, \(\overline y_{\mathrm{pre,tr}}\) is a \(T_{\mathrm{pre}}\)-vector and the design is
\[
X=[\,\mathbf1_{T_{\mathrm{pre}}}\ \ Y_{\mathrm{pre,co}}\,].
\]
Add a \emph{column} of ones to the predictors, not a row to the outcome. Fit \((w_0,w_{\mathrm{co}})\); constrain and penalize only the donor weights, not the intercept. By contrast, the row-vector time-weight convention on p. 8 correctly prepends a row of ones to \(Y_{\mathrm{pre,co}}\).

title: Estimate the scale from untreated pre-treatment data
diagnosis: The standard-deviation description omits the subset used to compute it.
correction: The standard SDID construction uses first differences of control-unit outcomes during the pre-treatment period to estimate \(\widehat\sigma\). Using treated post-intervention outcomes can let the effect influence the regularization scale. The positive fourth-root factor \((N_{\mathrm{tr}}T_{\mathrm{post}})^{1/4}\) in the notes is correct.

title: Unclear wording in the SDID intuition
diagnosis: The short handwritten phrase is ambiguous; the previous translation interpreted it as proximity to an expected treatment effect.
correction: The temporal reading above is plausible, but the middle characters remain unclear. Mathematically, time weights make weighted control pre-treatment outcomes predict control post-treatment outcomes; they do not select observations by closeness to an unknown treatment effect, and they need not select only recent periods.

title: SDID aside is about intervention timing
diagnosis: The previous English translation confidently said close to the expected treatment effect. The handwriting does not support that certainty.
correction: Use a cautious temporal reading and explicitly flag the unresolved middle phrase in orange.

title: Treatment-cell weights define the aggregate target
diagnosis: The decomposition weights are correct for averaging the included treated unit-period cells, but need a clearly stated target.
correction: The \(2/3,1/3\) weights count treated cells. Likewise, \(12/36\) and \(24/36\) average the California and three-other-unit effects over their observed treated durations, with equal period and unit weights. Other target populations can require different aggregation weights. Use genuinely untreated donor observations in each subpanel.

title: Precision is not uniformly better
diagnosis: The source says SDID has smaller error bars than SC without specifying a setting.
correction: SDID can improve precision and robustness in suitable designs; smaller valid standard errors than SC are not a universal guarantee. Estimated weights also contribute uncertainty, so an ordinary weighted-regression standard error is not automatically the SDID standard error.

title: Define the placebo mean and the interval convention
diagnosis: The source uses a b-indexed placebo mean and an undefined normal-quantile convention.
correction:
For \(B\) placebo estimates define \(\overline\tau^{\mathrm{pl}}=B^{-1}\sum_b\widehat\tau^{(b)}\) and
\[
\widehat V^{\mathrm{pl}}=B^{-1}\sum_b(\widehat\tau^{(b)}-\overline\tau^{\mathrm{pl}})^2.
\]
If \(z_p=\Phi^{-1}(p)\), the normal-approximation interval is \(\widehat\tau\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\widehat V^{\mathrm{pl}}}\). The handwritten \(z_{\alpha/2}\) can instead mean a positive upper-tail critical value; its convention is unstated. A confidence interval is a random set with a coverage claim, not a certainty that the realized interval contains \(\tau\).

title: Single-treated-unit placebo inference needs assumptions
diagnosis: Cycling through donor units is not enough by itself to justify a confidence interval for one treated unit.
correction: The placebo construction borrows noise information from controls. It needs comparable noise across units (the SDID paper requires cross-unit homoskedasticity for this argument), suitable donor samples, and a justified distributional approximation. It can fail when the treated unit has different noise variability. For more than one treated unit, each placebo assignment should reproduce the treated-group size.

title: The displayed extension is categorical
diagnosis: The handwritten label says continuous but the formula is a finite sum of point probabilities.
correction: This expression is for a discrete treatment with categories \(0,\ldots,K\). For a genuinely continuous dose, \(P(T=k\mid X)=0\) at an individual point in the usual continuous model; generalized propensity methods use a conditional density and require a separately specified dose-response estimand and estimator.

title: ATE and ATT weights differ
diagnosis: The displayed weights are ATE weights, while the intuitive target is the treated-group counterfactual.
correction: Under consistency, conditional exchangeability, and positivity, the displayed inverse-probability weights target ATE comparisons. For an ATT comparison, treated units receive weight 1 and controls receive \(e(X)/(1-e(X))\), with suitable normalization. A high-propensity control helps represent the treated covariate distribution, but it is not literally a treated unit.

title: Email example remains partly unreadable
diagnosis: The brief numerical example includes 20%, 0.2, email, and a 1, but the full assertion cannot be reconstructed confidently.
correction: The legible quantities are retained; no extra probability calculation or causal claim is inferred from the missing words.

title: Large weights and trimming
diagnosis: Small e does not inflate every observation weight; the warning about trimming needs its target-population consequence.
correction: For binary ATE weighting, small \(e\) inflates treated-unit weights \(1/e\), while \(e\) near one inflates control weights \(1/(1-e)\). Trimming can be a principled, prespecified response to limited overlap, but changes the population being studied and must be reported. Good propensity prediction alone does not establish causal exchangeability.
